prompt: What are the best practices for convolutional networks?
completion:
## Best‑Practice Checklist for Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) Below is a **systematic guide** that pulls together the most‑validated strategies for designing, training, evaluating, and deploying convolutional models. Feel free to cherry‑pick the items that fit your use‑case (image classification, detection, segmentation, video, medical imaging, etc.) and adapt them to your framework (PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX, etc.). | Category | Key Points | Practical Tips / Code | |----------|------------|----------------------| | **1. Data & Pre‑Processing** | • High‑quality, correctly labeled data is the single most critical factor.
• Reduce dataset bias & leakage. | • Use stratified splits (train/val/test).
• Ensure no augmentations leak test‑time information (e.g., no test‑time flips if you also flip train).
• Standardize pixel distribution: `x = (x - mean) / std` per channel.
• For small datasets, use strong augmentation pipelines (Albumentations, imgaug). | | **2. Model Architecture** | • **Receptive field** grows with depth; start with small kernels (3×3) and increase when necessary.
• **Weight sharing** & **local connectivity** reduce parameters.
• **Skip/Residual connections** mitigate vanishing gradients.
• **Depthwise separable** or **grouped** convolutions lower cost for mobile.
• **Global average pooling** before the classifier yields translation‑invariant predictions. | • `torchvision.models.resnet` or `efficientnet` for transfer learning.
• Use `nn.Conv2d` with `kernel_size=3`, `padding=1` to preserve spatial size.
• Add `nn.BatchNorm2d` + ReLU after each conv.
• For segmentation: `UNet`, `DeepLabV3`, `FPN` for multi‑scale. | | **3. Training Pipeline** | • **Optimizer**: SGD with momentum or AdamW (weight‑decay regularization).
• **Learning‑rate schedule**: cosine annealing, 1‑cycle, or step decay.
• **Batch size**: larger → more stable gradients; smaller → more regularization.
• **Mixed‑precision** (AMP) for speed & memory.
• **Gradient clipping** for stability on very deep nets. | ```python\nimport torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.optim as optim\nmodel = ...\noptimizer = optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1, momentum=0.9, weight_decay=1e-4)\nscheduler = optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(optimizer, T_max=90)\n# or use torch.optim.lr_scheduler.OneCycleLR\n``` | | **4. Regularization & Generalization** | • **Weight decay** (L2) & **dropout** (rarely used before conv layers).
• **Label smoothing** (0.1–0.2) combats over‑confidence.
• **CutMix / MixUp** blend images & labels for robust learning.
• **Early stopping** on validation loss. | ```python\n# label smoothing in loss\ncriterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(label_smoothing=0.1)\n``` | | **5. Evaluation & Validation** | • Track **accuracy, precision/recall, F1, ROC‑AUC** (classification).
• For segmentation: **IoU**, **Dice**, **Boundary F1**.
• Visualise **confusion matrix**, **Grad‑CAM** for model interpretability. | ```python\nfrom torchmetrics import Accuracy, ConfusionMatrix\nacc = Accuracy().to(device)\nconfmat = ConfusionMatrix(num_classes=10).to(device)\n``` | | **6. Deployment & Inference** | • **Quantization** (INT8) or **pruning** for edge devices.
• **ONNX/TensorRT** or **TorchScript** for production.
• Batch‑wise inference for GPU pipelines. | ```python\n# PyTorch 1.10+ quantization example\nmodel.qconfig = torch.quantization.get_default_qconfig('fbgemm')\nmodel = torch.quantization.prepare(model)\nmodel = torch.quantization.convert(model)\n``` | | **7. Reproducibility & Experiment Tracking** | • Fix seeds (`torch.manual_seed`, `numpy.random.seed`, `random.seed`).
• Log hyper‑parameters, code version, environment.
• Use tools: **Weights & Biases**, **MLflow**, **CometML**, **TensorBoard**. | ```python\nimport wandb\nwandb.init(project='cnn-best-practices', config=config)\n``` | | **8. Advanced / Emerging Techniques** | • **EfficientNet**: compound scaling of depth, width, resolution.
• **Vision Transformers (ViT)** and hybrids (CNN‑ViT, Swin Transformer).
• **Self‑supervised pre‑training** (SimCLR, MoCo) for small labeled datasets.
• **Auto‑ML / Neural Architecture Search** for optimal hyper‑parameters. | • `timm` library contains many pretrained efficient models. | --- ## Step‑by‑Step “How‑to” Example (PyTorch) ```python import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim import torchvision import timm # efficientnet, regnet, etc. from torch.cuda.amp import GradScaler, autocast # 1️⃣ Data train_tfms = torchvision.transforms.Compose([ torchvision.transforms.RandomResizedCrop(224), torchvision.transforms.RandomHorizontalFlip(), torchvision.transforms.ToTensor(), torchvision.transforms.Normalize(mean=[0.485,0.456,0.406], std =[0.229,0.224,0.225]), ]) val_tfms = torchvision.transforms.Compose([ torchvision.transforms.Resize(256), torchvision.transforms.CenterCrop(224), torchvision.transforms.ToTensor(), torchvision.transforms.Normalize(mean=[0.485,0.456,0.406], std =[0.229,0.224,0.225]), ]) train_ds = torchvision.datasets.CIFAR10(root='data', train=True, download=True, transform=train_tfms) val_ds = torchvision.datasets.CIFAR10(root='data', train=False, download=True, transform=val_tfms) train_dl = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(train_ds, batch_size=128, shuffle=True, num_workers=8, pin_memory=True) val_dl = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(val_ds, batch_size=128, shuffle=False, num_workers=8, pin_memory=True) # 2️⃣ Model (transfer‑learning) model = timm.create_model('efficientnet_b0', pretrained=True, num_classes=10) model = model.to('cuda') # 3️⃣ Optimizer & Scheduler optimizer = optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=3e-4, weight_decay=1e-4) scheduler = optim.lr_scheduler.OneCycleLR(optimizer, max_lr=3e-3, steps_per_epoch=len(train_dl), epochs=20) # 4️⃣ Mixed‑precision and loss scaler = GradScaler() criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(label_smoothing=0.1) # 5️⃣ Training loop for epoch in range(20): model.train() for xb, yb in train_dl: xb, yb = xb.to('cuda'), yb.to('cuda') optimizer.zero_grad() with autocast(): logits = model(xb) loss = criterion(logits, yb) scaler.scale(loss).backward() scaler.step(optimizer) scaler.update() scheduler.step() # Validation model.eval() val_loss = 0 correct = 0 total = 0 with torch.no_grad(): for xb, yb in val_dl: xb, yb = xb.to('cuda'), yb.to('cuda') with autocast(): logits = model(xb) loss = criterion(logits, yb) val_loss += loss.item() * xb.size(0) preds = logits.argmax(dim=1) correct += (preds == yb).sum().item() total += xb.size(0) print(f'Epoch {epoch+1:02d} | Val Acc: {correct/total:.4f} | Val Loss: {val_loss/total:.4f}') # 6️⃣ Save & Quantize torch.save(model.state_dict(), 'efficientnet_b0_cifar10.pth') model.qconfig = torch.quantization.get_default_qconfig('fbgemm') model = torch.quantization.prepare(model) model = torch.quantization.convert(model) torch.save(model.state_dict(), 'efficientnet_b0_cifar10_int8.pth') ``` > **Key take‑aways from the example** > * Transfer‑learning speeds up convergence and mitigates over‑fitting. > * One‑cycle LR schedule often beats a simple step decay. > * Label smoothing + MixUp (if you need stronger regularisation). > * Mixed‑precision reduces VRAM usage by ~30 % while keeping accuracy. --- ## Common Pitfalls & How to Avoid Them | Pitfall | Why it hurts | Fix | |---------|--------------|-----| | **Data leakage** | Validation metrics are optimistic. | Separate validation set before augmentation; use deterministic splits. | | **Over‑fitting to small datasets** | Model memorises training labels. | Use heavy augmentation, weight decay, early stopping, or pre‑training. | | **Learning‑rate mis‑tuning** | Too high → divergence, too low → slow convergence. | Use LR finder (fastai) or one‑cycle schedule. | | **Not using BatchNorm** | Internal covariate shift slows training. | Add BN after each conv and before activation. | | **Training on GPU with NaNs** | Unstable gradients. | Use gradient clipping, check for exploding values, lower LR. | | **Ignoring class imbalance** | Poor minority‑class performance. | Use focal loss, class‑weighting, or balanced batch sampling. | | **Deploying non‑quantized model on mobile** | Memory & latency bottleneck. | Apply post‑training quantization, pruning, or use efficient mobile nets. | --- ## Quick Reference Cheat‑Sheet | Topic | Best Practice | Example | |-------|---------------|---------| | **Weight init** | He normal for ReLU | `nn.init.kaiming_normal_(m.weight)` | | **Batch size** | 2^n (32, 64, 128) for stable LR scaling | `torch.utils.data.DataLoader(..., batch_size=64)` | | **Optimizer** | AdamW (weight decay) or SGD+Momentum | `optim.AdamW(...)` | | **Learning‑rate scheduler** | Cosine Annealing / One‑Cycle | `optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(...)` | | **Regularization** | Weight decay (1e-4), Label smoothing, MixUp | `nn.CrossEntropyLoss(label_smoothing=0.1)` | | **Augmentation** | RandCrop, Flip, ColorJitter, CutMix, MixUp | `torchvision.transforms.RandomResizedCrop(224)` | | **Mixed‑precision** | AMP | `torch.cuda.amp.autocast()` | | **Evaluation** | Top‑k, Confusion Matrix, Grad‑CAM | `torchmetrics.Accuracy(top_k=5)` | | **Deployment** | Quantize, ONNX, TorchScript | `torch.quantization.convert(...)` | | **Reproducibility** | Seed, deterministic ops | `torch.manual_seed(42)` | --- ## Bottom‑Line 1. **Start with a solid dataset** – no amount of network tweaking will compensate for bad data. 2. **Leverage pre‑trained models** – fine‑tuning beats training from scratch, especially on small data. 3. **Use standard training recipes** – SGD/AdamW + momentum + weight decay, with a learning‑rate schedule that “warms up” and cools down. 4. **Regularize aggressively** – label smoothing, CutMix/MixUp, weight decay, and early stopping. 5. **Validate rigorously** – track multiple metrics, visualise predictions, and sanity‑check on a held‑out set. 6. **Deploy smartly** – quantize, prune, or use a mobile‑friendly architecture for edge inference. 7. **Automate experiments** – log hyper‑parameters, code version, and results for reproducibility and faster iteration. Follow this checklist, iterate quickly, and you’ll see robust, state‑of‑the‑art CNN performance across most vision tasks. Happy training!
